title: Sensors and Actuators
subtitle: Reading temperature, ultrasonic distance, controlling motors and servos with PWM
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: An Arduino that can only blink an LED is useless in the real world. Real projects need to sense the environment (temperature, motion, distance) and act on it (move motors, trigger relays, drive servos).
whyItExists.solution: Sensor libraries abstract the low-level protocol details so you can focus on the application. Actuators are controlled via PWM, relay signals, or dedicated driver chips depending on current requirements.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any project that interacts with the physical world: weather stations, robots, smart doors, irrigation systems, and more.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If you only need logic/computation (no physical world interaction), you may not need any sensors — but that would be an unusual embedded project.

explainModes.beginner: Sensors are like the eyes and ears of your project — they convert temperature, distance, and motion into electrical signals your Arduino can read. Actuators are the hands — motors, servos, and buzzers that take action based on what the sensors report.
explainModes.simple: Most sensors use one of three interfaces: analog (a voltage that varies), digital (high/low pulses), or a data protocol (I2C/SPI/UART). Actuators are driven either by a GPIO pin directly (small current) or through a driver chip (high current motors).
explainModes.standard: The DHT22 uses a single-wire proprietary protocol. HC-SR04 uses trigger/echo pulse timing. Servo position is controlled by PWM pulse width (1–2 ms). DC motors above 500 mA need an H-bridge driver (L298N, TB6612). I2C sensors share the same two wires with device-specific addresses.
explainModes.technical: DHT22 pulls data low for a 50 µs start pulse, then sends 40 bits (16-bit humidity, 16-bit temp, 8-bit checksum) with bit encoding: 26-28 µs = 0, 70 µs = 1. HC-SR04 triggers a 40 kHz ultrasonic burst with a 10 µs pulse; echo pin is HIGH for the round-trip time. Servo PWM: 50 Hz signal, 1 ms = 0°, 1.5 ms = 90°, 2 ms = 180°.
explainModes.deepDive: Precision sensor reading requires ADC averaging (median filter to remove outliers), anti-alias filtering before ADC on rapidly-varying signals, and understanding reference voltage accuracy. The Arduino internal 1.1 V reference gives better ADC precision for 0–1.1 V sensors. For high-current loads (stepper motors), use dedicated drivers with current sensing (DRV8825, TMC2209) which offer micro-stepping and over-current protection.

content.text: The DHT22 (AM2302) is a popular digital temperature/humidity sensor. It uses a custom single-wire protocol; the DHT library handles all the timing. Accuracy: ±0.5°C temperature, ±2% humidity. It needs at least 2 seconds between readings.
The HC-SR04 measures distance by emitting a 40 kHz ultrasonic pulse and measuring how long the echo takes to return. Range: 2 cm – 400 cm, accuracy ±3 mm. It uses two pins: TRIG (trigger) and ECHO.
PWM: Controlling LED Brightness and Servos

PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) simulates analog output by rapidly switching a pin on and off. analogWrite(pin, 0–255) controls the duty cycle. Servo motors use a specific PWM signal: a 50 Hz signal where pulse width (1–2 ms) sets the angle.
Controlling DC Motors with an H-Bridge

A DC motor draws 100 mA–1 A — far more than a GPIO pin can provide (40 mA max). An H-bridge driver like the L298N or TB6612FNG acts as an amplifier, switching up to 2 A per channel from a motor supply rail while taking logic-level control signals.

Never connect a motor directly to an Arduino GPIO pin. Even small motors can draw 200–500 mA — this will instantly destroy the Arduino's voltage regulator or GPIO protection diodes. Always use a motor driver (L298N, L9110, TB6612FNG) with its own power supply.

questions.question: What is PWM used for in embedded systems?
options: Simulating analog output by varying pulse duty cycle to control brightness, speed, and position
questions.explanation: PWM rapidly switches a pin on/off. Varying the on-time (duty cycle) simulates an analog voltage. Used for LED brightness, motor speed, and servo position control.

questions.question: Why can't you connect a DC motor directly to an Arduino GPIO pin?
options: GPIO pins output AC not DC
Motors draw too much current (100mA–1A) — GPIO max is 40mA
Motors need 12V but Arduino runs at 5V
questions.explanation: GPIO pins are limited to 40 mA per pin. DC motors draw 100 mA–1 A, which would immediately damage the Arduino's output driver. Use an H-bridge like L298N.

questions.question: How does the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measure distance?
options: By measuring reflected infrared light intensity
By measuring the time between emitting an ultrasonic pulse and receiving its echo
By comparing two analog voltage levels
questions.explanation: HC-SR04 emits a 40 kHz ultrasonic burst and measures how long the echo takes to return. Distance = (echo duration × speed of sound) / 2.

faq.q: My DHT22 gives 'nan' readings. What's wrong?
faq.a: Common causes: (1) reading too fast — wait at least 2 seconds between reads; (2) no pull-up resistor on data pin — add 4.7 kΩ to Vcc; (3) wire too long — keep under 20 cm; (4) power supply noise — add 100 µF capacitor across Vcc and GND.

faq.q: How do I debounce a button?
faq.a: Add a 10–20 ms delay after detecting a state change, or use the Bounce2 library. For the millis() approach: record the time of the first edge, ignore further changes for 20 ms, then check the final state.

faq.q: What is the difference between a servo and a stepper motor?
faq.a: Servo: continuous rotation (360° DC motor) or limited rotation (hobby servo 0–180°). Easy to control with PWM. Stepper: moves in precise discrete steps (1.8° per step typically). Better for precise positioning (3D printer, CNC). More complex to drive but no feedback needed.
